newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S.-Russia summit will be hardest ever - Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-Russia summit will be hardest ever - Yeltsin.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin said on Friday that next week's Russia-U.S. summit in Helsinki would be the hardest since he became Russian president in 1991 and ruled out NATO membership for any former Soviet republics.
Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as telling Russian media chiefs, however, that he was ready for compromise at the meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton.

He ruled out any concessions which might threaten Russia's defence capability and said he wanted NATO to abandon any plans to offer membership to any of the 15 republics which made up the now defunct Soviet Union, singlijng out the three Baltic republics.
The talks "will be the hardest in all the history of Russian-American relations", Interfax quoted Yeltsin as saying.

But he added: "In a recent telephone conversation Clinton made clear the United States is interested in compromise, and so am I. We are for a compromise which would not abuse the security of the Russian Federation."
The row over NATO's plans to expand eastwards to take in former comunist-ruled countries in eastern and central Europe looks set to dominate the March 19-20 summit.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying differences could remain after the summit.
"We and the American side may disagree over questions of NATO expansion at the meeting in Helsinki but it is not worth making a tragedy out of this," it quoted him as saying.

Yeltsin said one "categoric condition" for Russia was that NATO should not try to draw in any of the 12 former Soviet republics which make up the loose Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) or the Baltic states Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia.

"In connection with this, the Russian leadership is alarmed by contacts between NATO and the leaderships of these countries, including the trip by alliance Secretary-General Javier Solana to a series of CIS states," Yeltsin said.
Solana has in recent weeks visited several CIS states.
Russia, which opposes NATO's plans to expand eastwards, particularly fears the security dangers if CIS member states join the alliance.
